summaries.example: Imagine two friends carrying a large box. One friend planning to lift it alone and the other friend planning to lift it alone does not make a shared plan. They have a shared intention when they understand that they are lifting the box together, each doing a part.
summaries.summary: Collective intentionality is what happens when several people direct their minds toward something together. They may plan a joint activity, notice the same object, accept a rule, believe something as a group, or share an emotion. Philosophers ask how this sharedness works. A group attitude cannot simply be a list of separate attitudes, yet no mysterious extra mind floats above the people. Different theories place the shared part in the goal, the special way people think as group members, or the group itself. These ideas help explain how people cooperate and how social things such as language, institutions, and money depend on what people accept together.
key_ideas: People can share plans, attention, beliefs, feelings, and goals.
Two people having matching private plans is not automatically a group plan.
Each person keeps their own mind, even when people think or act together.
Shared attitudes help create language, rules, money, teams, and other parts of social life.
summaries.why_it_matters: Much of everyday life depends on people acting as a “we.” Understanding shared intentions helps explain teamwork, friendships, classroom rules, institutions, and cooperation. It also raises an important question: how can people remain separate thinkers while creating something together?

important_terms.definition: When people’s minds are directed toward something together, such as a plan, belief, feeling, or goal.
A plan held by people who mean to do something together, not merely separate plans that happen to match.
Paying attention to the same thing while knowing that others are paying attention to it too.
The idea that a group attitude is more than a pile of separate individual attitudes.

questions_to_think_about: What makes two people’s plans a real team plan?
Can people share a feeling without talking about it?
Does everyone in a group need to agree for the group to have a belief?
How might shared plans help a class solve a problem?

summaries.example: Suppose two students decide to produce a science-fair project together. It is not enough that each independently intends to make a project, even if both know about the other’s plan. A shared intention requires some organized relation between their plans: each treats the project as joint, expects the other to contribute, and adjusts their own actions in response. Philosophers disagree about whether this structure is best explained by a shared content, a special “we-mode” of intending, or a group subject with its own organized decision process.
summaries.summary: Collective intentionality concerns ways in which people are mentally directed at something together: they may share an intention, attend jointly, accept a rule, hold a belief, or experience an emotion collectively. The entry’s central philosophical problem is a tension between two claims. Collective intentionality is not just a distribution or sum of individual attitudes; yet the attitudes must still belong to individual participants, since there is no need to posit a group super-mind. The debate explores where the collectivity is located. Content accounts emphasize that each person intends a joint activity. Mode accounts propose a distinctive form of group-member thinking, such as a we-mode or we-intention. Subject accounts ask whether a plural subject, organized group, or institution can itself bear intentions, beliefs, or emotions. The discussion also examines historical approaches, including social theory, phenomenology, and Sellars’s analysis of we-intentions. These issues matter because shared intentionality may help explain social institutions, collective responsibility, rational coordination, and distinctive human capacities for cooperation and communication.
key_ideas: The central problem is to reconcile irreducibility with individual ownership: shared intentionality is more than a sum, but individuals—not a group mind—have the attitudes.
The shared element might lie in content, mode, or subject. These are different answers to what exactly is collective.
Content-based accounts emphasize intending a joint activity; mode-based accounts emphasize a special group-member way of intending; subject accounts allow groups or plural subjects to bear attitudes.
Theories differ over the roles of mutual responsiveness, common or mutual belief, trust, expectations, obligations, and organized decision-making.
Collective intentionality connects philosophy of mind with social ontology, institutional facts, responsibility, coordination, and theories of human cooperation.
summaries.why_it_matters: Collective intentionality offers a bridge between individual minds and the social world. It helps us ask how paper becomes money, how a team becomes an agent, how people coordinate on conventions, and when responsibility can belong to a group. The debate also clarifies a lasting philosophical challenge: preserving individual autonomy while explaining genuine forms of togetherness.

important_terms.definition: The capacity of minds to be directed jointly toward objects, facts, goals, values, plans, beliefs, or emotions.
The claim that collective attitudes are not reducible to a mere aggregate of individual attitudes, even with common knowledge.
The claim that intentional states belong to individual agents and that each person retains their own mental autonomy.
What an intentional attitude is about, such as a joint activity or a proposition.
The kind of attitude involved, such as intending, believing, perceiving, hoping, or fearing.
The entity to which an attitude belongs or can be attributed as its bearer.
A way of having an attitude as a group member, contrasted with having it as a private individual.
A group-level commitment formed by participants together, which can generate mutual claims or obligations within the group.

questions_to_think_about: If two people independently choose the same action, what additional relation would make it joint action?
Can an individual intend that a group act without controlling the other members’ actions?
Are group beliefs merely shorthand for members’ beliefs, or can an organized group have beliefs of its own?
Do mutual obligations create joint action, or do they usually arise as a consequence of it?
Why might ordinary game theory give poor advice in situations where people must coordinate on one convention?

summaries.example: A group of students decides to make a short film. If each student separately wants to make a film, that is only a set of matching plans. It becomes a shared intention when they plan the film together, divide jobs, rely on one another, and understand that the final project is a joint activity. Still, philosophers may ask whether the “we” is part of the goal, part of the way each student thinks, or a feature of the group they form.
summaries.summary: Collective intentionality is the study of how people can think, feel, and act together. Examples include sharing a plan, paying attention to the same object, accepting a rule, believing something as a group, or grieving together. The central puzzle has two sides. A collective attitude must be more than separate individual attitudes placed side by side. For example, two people independently planning the same trip do not automatically plan a trip together. At the same time, each participant still has their own mind; the theory does not require a giant group brain. Philosophers have proposed several approaches. Content accounts say that participants intend a joint activity. Mode accounts say that people have a special way of thinking as group members, sometimes called the we-mode. Subject accounts ask whether an organized group or plural subject can itself have attitudes. The entry connects these questions with social institutions, group responsibility, coordination, and research about human cooperation.
key_ideas: Shared intention is different from two people having similar intentions and knowing about each other’s plans.
The main puzzle is how a group attitude can be genuinely shared without giving the group a separate mind that replaces its members.
Some philosophers focus on shared content, some on a special mode of group thinking, and some on groups as subjects.
Cooperation often involves expectations, mutual responsiveness, trust, or commitments, but philosophers disagree about which are necessary.
Collective attitudes may help explain institutions, conventions, responsibility, and why people can coordinate their actions.
summaries.why_it_matters: We constantly depend on shared understanding: teams need common plans, communities maintain rules, and institutions exist partly because people accept roles and meanings together. Studying collective intentionality helps explain how separate people can form a coordinated “we” without losing their individual viewpoints. It also shows why everyday cooperation can be philosophically difficult.

important_terms.definition: The ability of several people to aim their thoughts, plans, beliefs, or feelings at something together.
The view that a group’s shared attitude is not simply the total of separate attitudes held by its members.
The view that each person’s thoughts and intentions belong to that person, even during group activity.
The goal or thing an attitude is about, such as making a film together.
The type or style of attitude, such as believing, intending, fearing, or thinking as a group member.
The bearer of an attitude: an individual, a pair, or possibly an organized group.
Thinking or acting from the standpoint of being a member of a group rather than only as a private individual.

questions_to_think_about: What more is needed for two matching plans to count as one shared plan?
Can a person be part of a group intention while disagreeing about how to complete it?
When does a club or organization seem to have a belief of its own?
Are promises and obligations part of teamwork from the beginning, or do they develop afterward?
Why is following a traffic convention easier when people think from a shared point of view?
